title: R and Python together: penguin body mass by species and sex
text:
Data: Palmer Penguins, collected by Dr. Kristen Gorman at Palmer Station Antarctica LTER and released under CC0. Loaded from the palmerpenguins R package. Citation: Horst AM, Hill AP, Gorman KB (2020). palmerpenguins: Palmer Archipelago (Antarctica) penguin data. doi:10.5281/zenodo.3960218.
This post uses both languages in one document. R prepares the data, Python calculates the average body mass for each species and sex, and R takes that summary back to build a table and a chart. The two languages share one session through the reticulate package.

title: R and Python together: penguin body mass by species and sex
text:
Setup (R)

library(reticulate)
use_virtualenv("../../.venv", required = TRUE)

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)

title: R and Python together: penguin body mass by species and sex
R and Python together: penguin body mass by species and sex
text:
Summarise (Python)
Python reads the R data frame as r.penguins_clean, which arrives as a pandas DataFrame.

import pandas as pd

penguins = r.penguins_clean
print(type(penguins))

<class 'pandas.DataFrame'>

penguins["body_mass_kg"] = penguins["body_mass_g"] / 1000

summary = (
    penguins
    .groupby(["species", "sex"], observed=True)["body_mass_kg"]
    .agg(n="count", mean_kg="mean")
    .round(2)
    .reset_index()
)

title: R and Python together: penguin body mass by species and sex
text:
What I found
Table 1 and Figure 1 show that males are heavier than females in all three species, and that Gentoo penguins are the heaviest for both sexes. The averages were calculated in Python, and the table and chart were made in R from that same result.

title: Penguin body mass by species, in Python
text:
Visualise
Figure 1 shows the spread of body mass within each species.

species = sorted(penguins_clean["species"].unique())
masses = [penguins_clean.loc[penguins_clean["species"] == s, "body_mass_g"] for s in species]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.boxplot(masses, tick_labels=species)
ax.set_xlabel("Species")
ax.set_ylabel("Body mass (g)")
plt.show()







Figure 1: Body mass of penguins by species.






fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
for s, group in penguins_clean.groupby("species"):
    ax.scatter(group["flipper_length_mm"], group["body_mass_g"], label=s, alpha=0.7)
ax.set_xlabel("Flipper length (mm)")
ax.set_ylabel("Body mass (g)")
ax.legend(title="Species")
plt.show()







Figure 2: Flipper length against body mass, coloured by species.

title: Penguin body mass by species, in Python
text:
What I found
After dropping the 2 of 344 penguins with missing measurements, Gentoo penguins stand out as the heaviest species, averaging about 5,076 g, while Chinstrap (about 3,733 g) and Adelie (about 3,701 g) are nearly identical, differing by only about 30 g, which is small next to their spreads of roughly 400 to 450 g. The scatter plot shows that penguins with longer flippers tend to be heavier, and the Gentoo form their own distinct cluster with both longer flippers and greater mass than the other two species.

title: Penguin body mass by species and sex, in R
text:
What I found
Table 1 reproduces my Python result. Gentoo penguins are by far the heaviest, averaging about 5,076 g, while Chinstrap and Adelie are nearly identical at around 3,700 g. Table 2 and Figure 1 add the second question. In every species, males are heavier than females, and the gap is visible in the boxplot for all three. Sex is missing for a few birds, so those are left out of the sex comparison.
